name: diction_and_register
description: Word-level choice machinery: the etymological strata of English, register levels, connotation axes and loaded language, the interactional metadiscourse of hedges, boosters, attitude and engagement markers and self-mention, plus precision, verb-strength, naming, and figurative controls and the diction faults each one guards against.

etymological_layers.name: Anglo-Saxon core
etymological_layers.definition: The native Germanic stratum of English: the short, mostly monosyllabic words for body, weather, kin, work, and violence.
etymological_layers.example: hand, blood, bread, dark, break, hold, wife, dirt
etymological_layers.effect: Concrete, early-acquired, high-imagery; these words are processed fastest and felt hardest, which is why they carry punch and plainness.
etymological_layers.register: all registers; dominant in the plain and the intimate

etymological_layers.name: Latinate stratum
etymological_layers.definition: Words borrowed from Latin, directly or through French, typically polysyllabic and abstract.
etymological_layers.example: consideration, jurisdiction, facilitate, remuneration
etymological_layers.effect: Creates distance, generality, and institutional authority; the reader processes the concept without picturing anything.
etymological_layers.caution: A Latinate noun phrase can name a thing without committing to who did it — which is exactly why bureaucracies prefer it.

etymological_layers.name: Greek technical stratum
etymological_layers.definition: Scientific and scholarly vocabulary built from Greek roots and combining forms.
etymological_layers.example: photosynthesis, epistemology, hemorrhage, morpheme
etymological_layers.effect: Signals a specialist discourse and a defined term; a Greek-rooted word tells the reader this is a technical sense, not a loose one.

etymological_layers.name: Norman-French middle register
etymological_layers.definition: The stratum entering after 1066: government, law, cuisine, courtesy — sitting between Saxon plainness and Latin abstraction.
etymological_layers.example: judge, court, beef, mutton, courage, chamber — the classic pairing being Saxon animal to French meat: cow/beef, swine/pork, sheep/mutton
etymological_layers.effect: The polite, civil middle of English; formal without being clinical.

etymological_layers.name: Old Norse layer
etymological_layers.definition: Words from Scandinavian settlement, unusual in being everyday rather than learned.
etymological_layers.example: sky, skin, egg, knife, take, they, ugly, want
etymological_layers.effect: Blunt and plain; the sk- cluster in particular reads as hard-edged native English.

etymological_layers.name: etymological doublet
etymological_layers.definition: A pair of words with the same ultimate root that entered English by different routes and now differ in register.
etymological_layers.example: shirt/skirt, ward/guard, cattle/chattel, frail/fragile
etymological_layers.effect: Gives two settings for the same idea; the choice between them is almost pure register.

etymological_layers.name: Saxon-Latinate synonym pair
etymological_layers.definition: Two near-synonyms from the Germanic and Latin strata that differ chiefly in weight and warmth.
etymological_layers.example: ask/inquire, buy/purchase, end/terminate, help/assist, dead/deceased
etymological_layers.effect: The most common register lever in English prose; changing one member of the pair reprices the whole sentence.
etymological_layers.caution: Near-synonyms are rarely exact — deceased is not dead plus formality, it is dead plus a legal frame.

etymological_layers.name: lexical triplet
etymological_layers.definition: A three-way set from the Germanic, French, and Latin strata covering low, middle, and high register.
etymological_layers.example: kingly / royal / regal; rise / mount / ascend; ask / question / interrogate; fire / flame / conflagration
etymological_layers.effect: A ready-made three-position dial for elevation; the classic teaching example of how etymology maps onto register.

etymological_layers.name: legal binomial
etymological_layers.definition: A fixed pair joining a Germanic and a Romance term for the same thing, a survival of bilingual legal drafting.
etymological_layers.example: last will and testament; free and clear; goods and chattels; breaking and entering
etymological_layers.effect: Sounds inevitable and old; the redundancy is the point in law and pure ballast anywhere else.
etymological_layers.caution: Outside legal drafting, binomials are usually two words doing one word's work.

etymological_layers.name: phrasal verb
etymological_layers.definition: A Germanic verb plus particle functioning as a unit, usually with a single Latinate equivalent.
etymological_layers.example: put off / postpone; give up / relinquish; find out / ascertain; go into / investigate
etymological_layers.effect: Lowers the register and speeds the clause; the fastest way to make institutional prose sound like a person.
etymological_layers.caution: Phrasal verbs are often idiomatic and translate badly — a real cost in books meant for translation.

etymological_layers.name: inkhorn term
etymological_layers.definition: An ostentatiously learned coinage from Latin or Greek, in the sixteenth-century sense of the controversy and in the modern sense of pretension.
etymological_layers.example: obtestate, adnichilate, illecebrous
etymological_layers.effect: Signals learning at the cost of communication; the historical case study in why borrowed abstraction repels readers.
etymological_layers.caution: The modern equivalents are alive and well in management and academic prose.

etymological_layers.name: aureate diction
etymological_layers.definition: Deliberately gilded, Latin-heavy vocabulary used for elevation, especially in late-medieval and Renaissance verse.
etymological_layers.example: celestial, refulgent, mellifluate
etymological_layers.effect: Ceremonial elevation; still available for irony, almost never for sincerity.

etymological_layers.name: calque
etymological_layers.definition: A loan translation — a foreign compound rendered morpheme by morpheme rather than borrowed whole.
etymological_layers.example: loanword (from Lehnwort); flea market (from marche aux puces); worldview (from Weltanschauung)
etymological_layers.effect: Imports a foreign concept in native-looking clothes, so it reads as English while carrying a foreign shape of thought.

etymological_layers.name: unassimilated borrowing
etymological_layers.definition: A foreign word kept in its original form, often italicized, because English has no equivalent.
etymological_layers.example: schadenfreude, sprezzatura, ennui, sfumato
etymological_layers.effect: Names a concept precisely and flags that the concept is foreign; also flags the writer's range.
etymological_layers.caution: One per chapter is seasoning; three is a signal that the writer is performing rather than explaining.

etymological_layers.name: hybrid formation
etymological_layers.definition: A word combining roots or affixes from different strata.
etymological_layers.example: talkative (Germanic root, Latin suffix); beautiful (French root, Germanic suffix); television (Greek + Latin)
etymological_layers.effect: Proof that etymological purity is not a workable rule; useful against readers who object to a word on grounds of ancestry.

etymological_layers.name: Saxon monosyllable
etymological_layers.definition: The one-syllable native word chosen deliberately over a longer synonym.
etymological_layers.example: use, not utilize; end, not terminate; help, not facilitate
etymological_layers.effect: Direct, weighted, and hard to hide behind; each word takes its own stress, so the sentence gains rhythm as well as clarity.

etymological_layers.name: Latinate polysyllable
etymological_layers.definition: A long, abstract borrowing chosen for precision, elevation, or distance.
etymological_layers.example: commensurate, notwithstanding, interlocutory, provisional
etymological_layers.effect: Compresses a complicated relation into one token; the right choice when the concept genuinely is abstract.
etymological_layers.caution: Justified by precision, never by tone. If the plain word means the same thing, it is padding.

etymological_layers.name: plain-Saxon preference
etymological_layers.definition: The editorial rule of thumb — Orwell's fourth rule, and the plain-language movement generally — to prefer the short native word unless a longer one earns its place.
etymological_layers.example: Never use a long word where a short one will do. (Orwell, Politics and the English Language)
etymological_layers.effect: A reliable default that raises concreteness and lowers pomposity across a whole manuscript.
etymological_layers.caution: Applied mechanically it flattens genuine technical distinctions and produces a monotone of one-syllable words.

etymological_layers.name: nominal style
etymological_layers.definition: Prose that carries its content in Latinate nouns rather than verbs, so events become entities.
etymological_layers.example: The implementation of the reduction in expenditure was undertaken by the department.
etymological_layers.effect: Removes agency and time from the sentence; the standard shape of institutional writing.
etymological_layers.caution: The cure is to find the buried verb and give it a subject: The department cut spending.

etymological_layers.name: macaronic mixture
etymological_layers.definition: Deliberate blending of two languages within a sentence or text.
etymological_layers.example: Medieval sermons mixing Latin and English; contemporary Spanglish narration.
etymological_layers.effect: Marks a speaker who lives in both languages; in dialogue it does characterization no description can match.
etymological_layers.caution: Only convincing from inside the community it depicts.

etymological_layers.name: etymological fallacy
etymological_layers.definition: The mistake of treating a word's historical root as its real meaning.
etymological_layers.example: Insisting decimate can only mean reduce by a tenth, or that nice must mean ignorant.
etymological_layers.effect: Nothing good — it substitutes the writer's history lesson for the reader's understanding.
etymological_layers.caution: Etymology is a source of texture and connotation, never an authority about current meaning.

etymological_layers.name: semantic drift
etymological_layers.definition: The historical shift in a word's meaning: narrowing, broadening, amelioration, or pejoration.
etymological_layers.example: silly (blessed to foolish); awful (awe-inspiring to bad); girl (a young person of either sex to female)
etymological_layers.effect: Explains why quoting old sources requires glossing, and why period fiction needs a dated-sense check.

register_levels.name: frozen register
register_levels.definition: Language fixed by ritual or law and not rewritten for the occasion (Joos's first clock).
register_levels.example: the Lord's Prayer; the Miranda warning; a statute's operative text
register_levels.effect: Authority derived from invariance; quoting frozen language into prose imports its solemnity wholesale.

register_levels.name: formal register
register_levels.definition: Prepared, one-way, syntactically complete language addressed to an audience rather than an interlocutor.
register_levels.example: a keynote address; a judicial opinion; the front matter of a serious nonfiction book
register_levels.effect: Signals that the writer has thought before speaking; costs immediacy.

register_levels.name: consultative register
register_levels.definition: The standard register of informed conversation between people who do not share a private code: complete sentences, no slang, some contraction.
register_levels.example: a doctor explaining a diagnosis; most trade nonfiction narration
register_levels.effect: The workhorse register of published prose — formal enough to trust, loose enough to read.

register_levels.name: casual register
register_levels.definition: Language for people already inside the group: contractions, ellipsis, slang, shared reference.
register_levels.example: So we bailed. Nobody said anything.
register_levels.effect: Creates intimacy and speed; also excludes anyone outside the reference set.

register_levels.name: intimate register
register_levels.definition: Private language between people with a shared history: nicknames, fragments, in-jokes, unexplained reference.
register_levels.example: Not the blue one. You know.
register_levels.effect: In fiction it is the highest-bandwidth signal of closeness; on the page it must be legible to an outsider while sounding as if it were not written for one.

register_levels.name: grand style
register_levels.definition: The high style of classical rhetoric (genus grande): elevated diction, full periods, figures deployed openly, aimed at moving the audience.
register_levels.example: the peroration of a funeral oration
register_levels.effect: Moves; also risks bombast if the occasion does not carry it.
register_levels.caution: The grand style must be paid for by the subject. Applied to small matters it is the definition of bathos.

register_levels.name: middle style
register_levels.definition: The middle style (genus medium): moderate ornament, aimed at pleasing and holding attention.
register_levels.example: the familiar essay; feature journalism
register_levels.effect: Sustains a long text; the style most books are written in even when they visit the other two.

register_levels.name: plain style
register_levels.definition: The low or plain style (genus tenue): unornamented, aimed at teaching.
register_levels.example: instructions, procedure, technical explanation
register_levels.effect: Maximum clarity, minimum resistance; also the style whose plainness can be an argument in itself.
register_levels.caution: Plain is not the same as flat — the plain style still has cadence and still chooses its words.

register_levels.name: technical register
register_levels.definition: Vocabulary defined within a discipline where terms carry specified, narrow senses.
register_levels.example: In law, consideration; in statistics, significant; in physics, work.
register_levels.effect: Precision inside the field, misunderstanding outside it.
register_levels.caution: The dangerous terms are the ones that look like ordinary English — readers will import the everyday sense unless you gloss.

register_levels.name: academese
register_levels.definition: The house register of scholarly writing: nominalization, hedging, agentless passives, heavy citation-bearing syntax.
register_levels.example: It has been suggested that a degree of correlation may obtain between the variables in question.
register_levels.effect: Signals membership and caution; costs readability and often agency.
register_levels.caution: A trade book that keeps academic register loses the audience it was translated for.

register_levels.name: legalese
register_levels.definition: The drafting register of law: binomials, archaic deictics, defined terms, exhaustive qualification.
register_levels.example: hereinafter, aforesaid, notwithstanding the foregoing
register_levels.effect: Precision purchased with unreadability; sometimes a genuine trade, often an inherited habit.

register_levels.name: bureaucratese
register_levels.definition: Institutional prose that maximizes abstraction and minimizes attributable agency.
register_levels.example: Mistakes were made in the implementation of the revised guidance.
register_levels.effect: Diffuses responsibility; the register's core function, whether or not anyone intends it.
register_levels.caution: Quoting it is devastating; imitating it unawares is the commonest infection in policy writing.

register_levels.name: journalese
register_levels.definition: The compressed, formulaic register of news writing: stock epithets, headline nouns used as verbs, attribution formulas.
register_levels.example: slammed, blasted, amid growing concerns, sources close to
register_levels.effect: Fast and familiar; also a stock of dead phrases that survive because they fit a column width.

register_levels.name: corporate register
register_levels.definition: The vocabulary of management and consulting: agentless improvement verbs, abstract nouns of value, process metaphors.
register_levels.example: leverage, deliverable, operationalize, alignment, best-in-class
register_levels.effect: Signals membership in a professional culture; almost always reduces information per word.
register_levels.caution: Distinct from technical register in that its terms usually have no definitions to look up.

register_levels.name: vernacular
register_levels.definition: The everyday spoken language of a place or community, used in writing without translation into standard prose.
register_levels.example: regional idiom and syntax preserved in narration, not just in dialogue
register_levels.effect: Grounds a text in a specific speech community and refuses the standard-English default.

register_levels.name: colloquialism
register_levels.definition: An informal expression normal in speech and marked in formal writing.
register_levels.example: kind of, a lot, plenty, no big deal
register_levels.effect: Lowers distance; a few colloquialisms in an otherwise formal paragraph read as the writer stepping closer to the reader.

register_levels.name: slang
register_levels.definition: Vocabulary marking membership in a group and typically short-lived.
register_levels.example: the current generation's terms of approval, whatever they are this year
register_levels.effect: Immediate and dating; slang fixes a text to a moment.
register_levels.caution: In a book with a five-year shelf life, slang is a liability unless the moment is the subject.

register_levels.name: argot
register_levels.definition: The specialized and partly concealing vocabulary of a closed group — trade, criminal, or institutional.
register_levels.example: thieves' cant; carnival lingo; hospital shorthand
register_levels.effect: Powerful texture in reported nonfiction; each term should be glossed once and then trusted.

register_levels.name: dialect
register_levels.definition: A regional or social variety with its own lexicon, grammar, and pronunciation.
register_levels.example: Scots wee, ken; Appalachian a-fixing; AAVE habitual be
register_levels.effect: Characterizes precisely and economically when rendered through word choice and syntax.
register_levels.caution: Render dialect lexically and syntactically, not by respelling — eye dialect reads as mockery.

register_levels.name: code-switching
register_levels.definition: Moving between registers or languages within a text, often to mark a change of audience or role.
register_levels.example: A narrator who writes clinically about the procedure and colloquially about the waiting room.
register_levels.effect: Shows the speaker's range and the social position of each variety; a characterization device in its own right.

register_levels.name: register clash
register_levels.definition: Deliberate collision of a high and low register in the same sentence.
register_levels.example: The Board resolved, unanimously and after due deliberation, to punt.
register_levels.effect: Comedy, irony, or deflation depending on which direction the drop runs; bathos is the descending case.

register_levels.name: register drift
register_levels.definition: Unintentional slide from one register into another across a passage.
register_levels.example: A formal argument that shifts into blog voice for two sentences and back.
register_levels.effect: Breaks the reader's model of who is speaking.
register_levels.caution: Most often introduced during revision, when new sentences are written in a different mood than the draft.

register_levels.name: house style
register_levels.definition: A publisher's or publication's codified preferences on spelling, punctuation, numbers, and usage.
register_levels.example: serial comma; -ize versus -ise; whether contractions are permitted
register_levels.effect: Consistency the reader never notices until it breaks.
register_levels.caution: House style governs mechanics; it does not govern voice, and confusing the two flattens a book.

connotation_axes.name: concrete to abstract
connotation_axes.definition: The axis from words naming perceptible things to words naming categories and relations.
connotation_axes.effect: Concreteness raises imageability, memory, and credibility; abstraction buys scope. Most weak prose sits one rung too high.

connotation_axes.name: general to specific
connotation_axes.definition: The taxonomic axis from superordinate to basic-level to subordinate terms.
connotation_axes.effect: The basic level (car, dog, chair) is the fastest to process; going below it signals expertise and observed detail.

connotation_axes.name: warm to clinical
connotation_axes.definition: The axis between words that engage feeling and words that hold it off.
connotation_axes.example: died / passed away / expired / experienced mortality
connotation_axes.effect: Clinical diction is the standard instrument of professional distance; it can be humane or evasive depending on who is protected by it.

connotation_axes.name: formal to casual
connotation_axes.definition: The axis of social distance encoded in vocabulary.
connotation_axes.effect: Sets how far the writer is standing from the reader, independent of what is being said.

connotation_axes.name: archaic to current
connotation_axes.definition: The axis of a word's felt datedness.
connotation_axes.example: whilst / while; wireless / radio; icebox / fridge
connotation_axes.effect: Dated vocabulary evokes a period and a class; a single archaism in modern prose reads as either texture or affectation.

connotation_axes.name: common to rare
connotation_axes.definition: The frequency axis, which governs processing effort and the sense that a word has been chosen.
connotation_axes.effect: Rare words are noticed; that attention is a resource, spent well on the sentence's key term and wasted on its connectives.

connotation_axes.name: plain to ornate
connotation_axes.definition: The axis of decorative elaboration in word choice.
connotation_axes.example: the sea / the wine-dark sea / the illimitable azure deep
connotation_axes.effect: Ornament signals occasion; unearned ornament signals insecurity.

connotation_axes.name: native to foreign
connotation_axes.definition: How assimilated a word feels to English.
connotation_axes.example: kill / execute / liquidate; feeling / sentiment / affect
connotation_axes.effect: Foreign-feeling words carry either expertise or evasion, and readers register which.

connotation_axes.name: neutral to loaded
connotation_axes.effect: Loaded terms perform the argument before it is made, which is why an honest argument makes its own loading visible.

connotation_axes.name: literal to figurative
connotation_axes.definition: How far a word has traveled from its physical sense.
connotation_axes.example: grasp a rope / grasp an idea; a bright light / a bright student
connotation_axes.effect: Faded metaphors are invisible and useful; live ones are visible and must be governed.

connotation_axes.name: monosyllabic to polysyllabic
connotation_axes.definition: The length axis, which controls both weight and pace.
connotation_axes.effect: Short words land, long words glide; the same content changes speed entirely with the swap.

connotation_axes.name: human to institutional agency
connotation_axes.definition: Whether the sentence's actors are people or entities.
connotation_axes.example: the nurse decided / the ward decided / policy dictated
connotation_axes.effect: Institutional agents make responsibility disappear; naming the human restores it, sometimes unfairly.

connotation_axes.name: semantic prosody
connotation_axes.definition: The evaluative coloring a word acquires from the company it habitually keeps, independent of its dictionary meaning.
connotation_axes.example: cause takes bad outcomes (cause harm, cause delay); commit takes offenses; utterly takes negatives.
connotation_axes.effect: Explains why a technically correct word can feel wrong; corpus evidence, not intuition, is the way to check.
connotation_axes.caution: Machine-generated prose frequently violates semantic prosody in ways that read as subtly off.

connotation_axes.name: collocational strength
connotation_axes.definition: How strongly a word expects particular neighbors.
connotation_axes.example: strong tea but powerful engine; heavy rain but strong wind
connotation_axes.effect: Getting collocation wrong is the surest marker of a non-native or a thesaurus-assisted sentence.

loaded_language.name: orthophemism
loaded_language.definition: The direct, neutral term between the euphemism and the dysphemism.
loaded_language.example: died, between passed away and croaked
loaded_language.effect: The default for honest exposition; naming this middle term makes the other two visible as choices.

loaded_language.name: purr word
loaded_language.definition: A term whose positive charge does the persuading without any propositional content.
loaded_language.effect: Attracts assent before an argument exists.
loaded_language.caution: If deleting the word changes no fact, it was doing evaluative work you have not defended.

loaded_language.name: snarl word
loaded_language.definition: The negative counterpart: a term that condemns without describing.
loaded_language.effect: Costs nothing to deploy and cannot be rebutted, because there is no claim in it.

loaded_language.name: dog whistle
loaded_language.definition: A term with a mainstream surface meaning and a second meaning legible to a target audience.
loaded_language.example: coded appeals whose deniability is the point
loaded_language.effect: Two audiences read two messages, and the speaker can disown one.

loaded_language.name: thought-terminating cliche
loaded_language.definition: A stock phrase deployed to close an inquiry rather than answer it.
loaded_language.example: It is what it is. Everything happens for a reason. That's just human nature.
loaded_language.effect: Ends discussion by supplying the feeling of an explanation.
loaded_language.caution: Easy to write unawares at the end of a hard paragraph — check every paragraph-closing aphorism.

loaded_language.name: ideograph
loaded_language.definition: A high-order abstraction that a culture treats as self-justifying warrant for policy (McGee).
loaded_language.example: liberty, security, the rule of law, property
loaded_language.effect: Carries enormous persuasive force with almost no fixed content, so arguments are often fought over which ideograph applies.

loaded_language.name: rhetorical redefinition
loaded_language.definition: Renaming a thing so that the new label carries a different evaluation.
loaded_language.example: estate tax / death tax; undocumented / illegal; enhanced interrogation / torture
loaded_language.effect: The most consequential single-word move in public argument; whoever fixes the name usually wins the frame.
loaded_language.caution: In nonfiction, name your own choice explicitly and say why, rather than pretending one label is neutral.

loaded_language.name: hedged attribution
loaded_language.definition: Words that assign a claim to unnamed others so the writer carries none of it.
loaded_language.example: critics say, some argue, it is widely believed
loaded_language.effect: Imports a position without an owner or a source.
loaded_language.caution: A weasel construction unless the some can be named. Name them or drop the claim.

loaded_language.name: honorific and title choice
loaded_language.definition: The decision of how to name a person — full name, surname, first name, title, or role — and how consistently.
loaded_language.example: Dr. King / King / Martin / the Reverend
loaded_language.effect: Encodes deference, intimacy, and status; inconsistency across people in the same book encodes bias.
loaded_language.caution: Audit surname-versus-first-name usage across genders and races; this is a standard editorial check.

loaded_language.name: people-first and identity-first phrasing
loaded_language.definition: The choice between naming the person before the attribute and naming the attribute as identity.
loaded_language.example: a person with autism / an autistic person; a person experiencing homelessness / a homeless person
loaded_language.effect: Communities differ in preference, and the choice is read as a statement about whose usage you follow.
loaded_language.caution: There is no universally safe default; follow the usage of the community you are writing about and be consistent.

hedges.name: epistemic modal
hedges.definition: A modal auxiliary marking a claim as possible rather than certain.
hedges.example: The delay may have cost the project its funding.
hedges.effect: Lowers commitment to the proposition while leaving the claim on the table.

hedges.name: epistemic adverb
hedges.definition: A sentence adverb encoding the writer's degree of confidence.
hedges.example: Arguably, the second audit was the only one that mattered.
hedges.effect: Places the qualification outside the proposition, so the claim can still be read as a claim.
hedges.caution: Arguably in particular has become a tic that means nothing; delete it and see whether the sentence weakens.

hedges.name: tentative reporting verb
hedges.definition: A lexical verb that presents a finding as indication rather than proof.
hedges.example: The records suggest that the transfers began earlier.
hedges.effect: The standard academic hedge; commits to a direction without committing to a fact.

hedges.name: quantity approximator
hedges.definition: A qualifier that makes a numeric or quantitative claim inexact on purpose.
hedges.example: roughly four thousand pages of discovery
hedges.effect: Honest imprecision; signals that the exact figure is either unknown or not the point.
hedges.caution: Approximating a number you actually have throws away your best evidence.

hedges.name: frequency approximator
hedges.definition: A qualifier limiting how often a generalization holds.
hedges.example: Auditors typically stop at the first clean quarter.
hedges.effect: Converts a universal claim into a defensible tendency.

hedges.name: degree downtoner
hedges.definition: A qualifier reducing the intensity of an adjective or verb.
hedges.example: a somewhat unusual arrangement
hedges.effect: Softens evaluation.
hedges.caution: The commonest padding in draft prose; two downtoners in one sentence cancel the sentence.

hedges.name: plausibility shield
hedges.definition: An impersonal construction attributing the appearance of a fact to the evidence rather than to the writer.
hedges.example: It appears that no one signed off.
hedges.effect: Removes the writer as the source of the judgment while still making it.

hedges.name: attribution shield
hedges.definition: Assigning a claim to a named source so its truth is the source's responsibility.
hedges.example: According to the inspector general, the figures had been revised twice.
hedges.effect: The honest form of hedging: the reader can go check.
hedges.caution: Only a shield if the source is nameable and named — otherwise it is a weasel construction.

hedges.name: evidential hedge
hedges.definition: A marker of how the writer came to know, which implicitly limits how far the claim can be trusted.
hedges.example: The meeting reportedly lasted twenty minutes.
hedges.effect: Signals second-hand knowledge; legally load-bearing in journalism.

hedges.name: impersonal hedge
hedges.definition: An extraposed construction that states a possibility without a subject who holds it.
cues: it may be the case that
hedges.example: It is possible that the two events are unrelated.
hedges.effect: Maximum distance between writer and claim.
hedges.caution: Wordy by construction; usually replaceable by a single modal.

hedges.name: agentless passive hedge
hedges.definition: A passive that deletes the agent so no one owns the claim or the act.
hedges.example: Concerns were raised about the timeline.
hedges.effect: Hides who raised them, which is sometimes protection and often evasion.
hedges.caution: Ask by whom. If you can answer, name them.

hedges.name: conditional hedge
hedges.definition: A conditional clause that makes the claim contingent on an assumption.
hedges.example: If the timestamps are accurate, the sequence is impossible.
hedges.effect: Exposes the load-bearing assumption instead of burying it — the most intellectually honest hedge available.

hedges.name: scope restrictor
hedges.definition: A qualifier limiting the domain over which a claim is asserted.
cues: at least in the United States
hedges.example: Among the firms surveyed, none had a written policy.
hedges.effect: Narrows the claim to what the evidence supports; a restrictor added late in revision usually rescues an overreach.

hedges.name: limitation statement
hedges.definition: An explicit statement of what the evidence or method cannot show.
hedges.example: These records cannot establish intent; they establish only sequence.
hedges.effect: Builds credibility by pre-empting the strongest objection; the reader who was about to distrust you now does not.

hedges.name: numerical range
hedges.definition: Reporting an interval or an order of magnitude instead of a point estimate.
hedges.example: on the order of ten thousand claims
hedges.effect: Communicates precision about your imprecision — more trustworthy than a false-precision single number.

hedges.name: hedged performative
hedges.definition: Softening the speech act itself rather than the proposition.
hedges.example: I would suggest a simpler reading.
hedges.effect: Politeness marker; lowers the social cost of disagreement.
hedges.caution: In a book-length argument it reads as apologizing for having a thesis.

hedges.name: self-limiting knowledge claim
hedges.definition: An explicit statement of the boundary of the writer's own knowledge.
cues: as far as I can tell
I have found no evidence that
hedges.example: As far as I can tell, no one has looked at the second set of ledgers.
hedges.effect: Converts an absence of evidence into a checkable statement about the search rather than the world.

hedges.name: hypothetical framing
hedges.definition: Using irrealis mood or counterfactual grammar to entertain a claim without asserting it.
hedges.example: Suppose the second signature was forged.
hedges.effect: Lets an argument run a scenario at full strength without adopting it.

hedges.name: scare quotes
hedges.definition: Quotation marks used to distance the writer from a term's aptness rather than to quote a source.
hedges.example: the department's 'review' of its own conduct
hedges.effect: Registers skepticism in one keystroke.
hedges.caution: Cheap and unfalsifiable — it sneers without arguing. Once per chapter, and only where the objection is obvious.

hedges.name: epistemic adjective
hedges.definition: An adjective encoding likelihood or uncertain status.
hedges.example: the putative author of the memo
hedges.effect: Hedges inside a noun phrase, where a modal cannot reach.

hedges.name: compound hedge
hedges.definition: Two or more hedges stacked on the same proposition.
hedges.example: It may perhaps be somewhat possible that the delay was a factor.
hedges.effect: Each hedge multiplies the uncertainty until nothing is claimed.
hedges.caution: A defining feature of unconfident draft prose. Keep the one hedge that carries real doubt and cut the rest.

hedges.name: hedge inflation
hedges.definition: Sustained high hedge density across a text, independent of any actual uncertainty.
hedges.example: A chapter where nearly every claim carries a modal or a downtoner.
hedges.effect: Readers stop reading the hedges as information and start reading them as timidity; genuine uncertainty then goes unnoticed.
hedges.caution: Measurable per thousand words; hedge density is the core number in a register report.

boosters.name: certainty adverb
boosters.definition: A sentence adverb asserting that the claim is beyond reasonable doubt.
boosters.example: The transfer was clearly timed to the announcement.
boosters.effect: Raises commitment and closes the question.
boosters.caution: Clearly and obviously most often appear where the argument is weakest — they ask the reader to agree instead of showing why.

boosters.name: factive verb
boosters.definition: A reporting verb that presupposes the truth of what follows.
boosters.example: The audit established that the funds had moved twice.
boosters.effect: Commits the writer fully; the strongest ordinary way to endorse a finding.
boosters.caution: Using a factive verb for a contested claim is an unearned booster a careful reader will catch.

boosters.name: amplifier
boosters.definition: An adverb intensifying a gradable adjective or verb.
boosters.caution: Usually the sign that the adjective is too weak. Replace very tired with exhausted, not with very very tired.

boosters.name: maximizer
boosters.definition: An adverb asserting the top of a scale.
boosters.effect: Removes any remaining degree; rhetorically forceful and easy to disprove with one counterexample.

boosters.name: universal quantifier
boosters.definition: A quantifier claiming that a proposition holds without exception.
boosters.example: No one at the firm asked where the money came from.
boosters.effect: The strongest claim available in ordinary language and therefore the easiest to falsify.
boosters.caution: Every universal in a nonfiction manuscript is a hostage. Check that you can defend each one.

boosters.name: emphatic do
boosters.definition: The auxiliary do inserted into an affirmative clause for emphasis.
boosters.example: He did read the memo. He read it twice.
boosters.effect: Contradicts an expectation the reader is presumed to hold; carries a whole implied argument in one word.

boosters.name: assumed-consensus booster
boosters.definition: A phrase asserting that agreement already exists.
boosters.example: It goes without saying that the deadline was arbitrary.
boosters.effect: Makes disagreement socially costly rather than argumentatively costly.
boosters.caution: If it goes without saying, cut it. If it does not, prove it.

boosters.name: factive framing
boosters.definition: A frame presenting the following clause as established reality.
boosters.example: The reality is that no one was going to read the report.
boosters.effect: Smuggles a contested claim in as a premise.
boosters.caution: The fact that is also a wordiness marker; nine times in ten the sentence is stronger without the frame.

boosters.name: concessive booster
boosters.definition: A connective that raises commitment by contrast with an expected weaker reading.
boosters.example: The system was not merely slow; indeed, it had stopped.

boosters.name: superlative
boosters.definition: A claim to the top of a comparison class.
boosters.example: the largest single transfer in the account's history
boosters.effect: Newsworthy by construction, which is why superlatives attract fact-checkers.
boosters.caution: Every superlative requires a stated comparison class or it is decoration.

boosters.name: absolute adjective
boosters.definition: An adjective that admits no degrees but is frequently used as though it did.
boosters.effect: Strong when accurate; when hedged (rather unique) it announces that the writer did not mean it.

boosters.name: typographic emphasis
boosters.definition: Italics, bold, or capitals used to boost a word beyond what the syntax gives it.
boosters.example: He said he would handle it.
boosters.caution: Print convention allows very little of this; more than a few per chapter reads as shouting or as unrewritten drafting.

boosters.name: repetition booster
boosters.definition: Repeating a word or clause so that the repetition itself asserts importance.
boosters.example: It was late. Late by a year, late by two budgets, late by the time anyone noticed.
boosters.effect: Emphasis without any intensifier; the strongest booster that adds rather than inflates.

boosters.name: precision booster
boosters.definition: Replacing an intensifier with an exact figure or detail.
boosters.example: Not: an enormous backlog. But: 41,000 unread claims.
boosters.effect: The number does the work the adjective was trying to do, and it can be checked.
boosters.caution: Requires you actually to have the number; false precision is worse than the adjective.

boosters.name: litotes
boosters.definition: Affirmation by denial of the contrary — understatement that reads as strong assertion.
boosters.effect: Dry emphasis; carries a raised eyebrow the plain assertion lacks.
boosters.caution: A signature of British register and of academic irony; overuse produces prose that never says anything straight.

boosters.name: expletive intensifier
boosters.definition: Profanity or taboo language used purely as an intensifier.
boosters.example: reported speech where the intensifier is the point
boosters.caution: Sets the book's register permanently at the first occurrence; decide in the style sheet, not mid-draft.

boosters.name: flat assertion
boosters.definition: The unhedged, unboosted declarative — the strongest position available because it does not argue about its own strength.
boosters.effect: Maximum authority at minimum cost; boosters weaken it by suggesting it needed help.
boosters.caution: Only usable where the evidence is already on the page.

boosters.name: booster inflation
boosters.definition: Sustained high booster density, so that ordinary claims arrive at maximum volume.
boosters.example: A chapter in which nearly every finding is critical, essential, or profound.
boosters.effect: The reader recalibrates downward, and the genuinely important claim now reads as routine.
boosters.caution: Trackable per thousand words alongside hedge density; the two together profile a text's stance.

attitude_markers.name: evaluative sentence adverb
attitude_markers.definition: An adverb expressing the writer's affective response to the whole proposition.
attitude_markers.effect: Tells the reader how to feel about a fact before they have finished reading it.
attitude_markers.caution: One per paragraph is a voice; three is editorializing that the evidence has not earned.

attitude_markers.name: importance marker
attitude_markers.definition: A marker asserting that an item deserves attention.
attitude_markers.example: Crucially, the second memo was never circulated.
attitude_markers.caution: If everything is crucial, the marker is noise. Use it to break a tie, not to open a paragraph.

attitude_markers.name: affective adjective
attitude_markers.definition: An adjective carrying the writer's evaluation rather than a property of the thing.
attitude_markers.example: an alarming gap in the record
attitude_markers.effect: Fastest route to stance; also the fastest route to telling instead of showing.
attitude_markers.caution: If the fact is alarming, the reader will supply the adjective; supplying it yourself invites resistance.

attitude_markers.name: deontic modal
attitude_markers.definition: A modal expressing obligation, necessity, or desirability rather than probability.
attitude_markers.example: The rule should never have applied to volunteers.
attitude_markers.effect: Moves from describing to prescribing, and commits the writer to a normative position.

attitude_markers.name: scalar even
attitude_markers.definition: The particle even, marking an item as unexpected at the far end of a scale.
attitude_markers.example: Even the auditors did not have access.
attitude_markers.effect: Encodes a whole implicit ranking in three letters; the reader infers everyone else lacked access too.

attitude_markers.name: limiting particle
attitude_markers.definition: A particle marking an item as less than expected.
attitude_markers.example: The fine came to just eight thousand dollars.
attitude_markers.effect: Evaluates by scale rather than by adjective.
attitude_markers.caution: Placement changes the meaning; only migrates in drafts and lands on the wrong constituent.

attitude_markers.name: evaluative noun
attitude_markers.definition: A noun whose choice performs a judgment on the event it names.
attitude_markers.effect: Buries the verdict inside the reference, where it is harder to dispute than a stated claim.
attitude_markers.caution: In reported nonfiction this is the main place bias enters unnoticed.

attitude_markers.name: skeptical reporting verb
attitude_markers.definition: A reporting verb that signals doubt about the reported claim.
attitude_markers.example: The company claims the data was anonymized.
attitude_markers.caution: Claim and said are not interchangeable; a fact-checker will read your reporting verbs as your position.

attitude_markers.name: endorsing reporting verb
attitude_markers.definition: A reporting verb that signals agreement with the reported claim.
attitude_markers.example: As the inspector points out, the dates do not line up.
attitude_markers.effect: Aligns the writer with the source; point out in particular presupposes the point is correct.

attitude_markers.name: irony marker
attitude_markers.definition: A word or device flagging that the label is being used at arm's length.
attitude_markers.caution: Sarcasm in nonfiction ages badly and costs credibility faster than it buys agreement.

attitude_markers.name: emphatic negation
attitude_markers.definition: Negative adverbs and quantifiers that carry attitude as well as denial.
attitude_markers.effect: Denies and evaluates at once; typically dry rather than heated.

attitude_markers.name: value-laden comparative
attitude_markers.definition: A comparative that ranks and judges in the same phrase.
attitude_markers.example: Worse still, the backups had been deleted.
attitude_markers.effect: Chains evaluations into an escalating series.
attitude_markers.caution: The classic transition of outrage writing; it can carry a paragraph past the evidence.

attitude_markers.name: understatement
attitude_markers.definition: Deliberately describing something as smaller or milder than it is, leaving the reader to correct upward.
attitude_markers.example: Losing the only copy was inconvenient.
attitude_markers.effect: Trusts the reader, which flatters them; the resulting judgment feels like theirs.

attitude_markers.name: exclamatory attitude
attitude_markers.definition: Syntax or punctuation carrying evaluation directly — exclamations, inversions, interjections.
attitude_markers.example: What a way to run an audit.
attitude_markers.effect: Voice at full volume; rare in expository prose and conspicuous when it appears.
attitude_markers.caution: One per book, at most, in serious nonfiction.

attitude_markers.name: attitude leakage
attitude_markers.definition: Evaluative language arriving before the evidence that would justify it.
attitude_markers.example: Calling a decision indefensible in the sentence that first describes it.
attitude_markers.effect: Readers who have not yet seen the facts feel managed and start resisting.
attitude_markers.caution: Order matters more than intensity: earn the adjective, then use it, or let the facts stand and skip it.

engagement_markers.name: reader pronoun
engagement_markers.definition: Direct second-person address to the reader.
engagement_markers.example: You have signed one of these without reading it.
engagement_markers.effect: Collapses distance and implicates the reader in the subject.
engagement_markers.caution: Register-defining. Once you address the reader in chapter one, you cannot stop in chapter six.

engagement_markers.name: inclusive we
engagement_markers.definition: First-person plural including the reader in the writer's reasoning.
engagement_markers.example: We have been assuming the timestamps are reliable.
engagement_markers.effect: Makes an argument feel jointly conducted rather than delivered.
engagement_markers.caution: Presumptuous when the we asserts shared values rather than shared reasoning.

engagement_markers.name: directive
engagement_markers.definition: An imperative telling the reader to perform a cognitive act.
engagement_markers.effect: The most common engagement move in academic and expository prose; steers attention without addressing the reader personally.

engagement_markers.name: physical-act directive
engagement_markers.definition: An imperative asking the reader to do something outside the text.
engagement_markers.example: Look at the second column of the table.
engagement_markers.effect: Points at evidence; in a book, mostly directs the eye to a figure or an appendix.

engagement_markers.name: rhetorical question
engagement_markers.definition: A question posed for effect rather than to elicit an answer.
engagement_markers.example: Who was supposed to be watching?
engagement_markers.effect: Enlists the reader in reaching a conclusion they now feel they reached themselves.
engagement_markers.caution: A question the next sentence immediately answers is filler. It also stacks: three in a paragraph and the prose reads as a sermon.

engagement_markers.name: shared-knowledge appeal
engagement_markers.definition: An assertion that a piece of knowledge is already common between writer and reader.
engagement_markers.example: The familiar version of the story ends there.
engagement_markers.effect: Builds an in-group; also excludes the reader who does not know.
engagement_markers.caution: Every shared-knowledge appeal is a bet about your audience. Wrong bets read as condescension.

engagement_markers.name: hypothetical second person
engagement_markers.definition: Putting the reader inside a scenario as its agent.
engagement_markers.example: Imagine you are the clerk who takes the call.
engagement_markers.effect: Converts an abstract problem into a decision the reader has to make; the most efficient empathy device in expository prose.

engagement_markers.name: aside to the reader
engagement_markers.definition: A brief break from the argument to speak to the reader directly about the text itself.
engagement_markers.example: This is the part I got wrong in the first edition.
engagement_markers.effect: Reveals the writer as a person and resets attention.
engagement_markers.caution: Only works if the persona is already established; otherwise it reads as intrusion.

engagement_markers.name: anticipated objection
engagement_markers.definition: Voicing the reader's likely counter before making the next move.
engagement_markers.example: You might think the dates settle it. They do not.
engagement_markers.effect: Shows the writer has heard the objection, which buys the credit needed to answer it.

engagement_markers.name: hortative
engagement_markers.definition: A first-person plural invitation to act or proceed together.
engagement_markers.example: Let me take the weaker version of the claim first.
engagement_markers.effect: Signposts a move and frames it as a shared decision.
engagement_markers.caution: Very high register; in casual voices let us reads as a lecture hall.

engagement_markers.name: reader-role address
engagement_markers.definition: Naming the reader's presumed role and speaking to it.
engagement_markers.example: If you run a small nonprofit, this is where the exposure begins.
engagement_markers.effect: Segments the audience and raises stakes for the segment addressed.

engagement_markers.name: appeal to reader experience
engagement_markers.definition: Invoking an experience the reader is presumed to have had.
engagement_markers.example: Anyone who has ever waited on hold with a state agency knows the sound.
engagement_markers.effect: Grounds an abstraction in a memory the reader supplies themselves.
engagement_markers.caution: The presumed experience is class-marked more often than writers notice.

engagement_markers.name: permission to skip
engagement_markers.definition: Explicitly telling the reader that a passage can be skipped or is for specialists.
engagement_markers.example: Readers who know the statute can skip to the next section.
engagement_markers.effect: Respects the reader's time and lets a book serve two audiences at once.

engagement_markers.name: code gloss
engagement_markers.definition: An in-line restatement or definition supplied so the reader can decode a term.
engagement_markers.example: The account was in escrow — that is, no one could touch it without both signatures.
engagement_markers.effect: The main device for using a technical term once and keeping the general reader.
engagement_markers.caution: Glossing something the reader already understands is condescension; glossing twice is worse.

engagement_markers.name: endophoric directive
engagement_markers.definition: A pointer to another part of the same text.
engagement_markers.example: The second problem, described in chapter 4, is worse.
engagement_markers.effect: Builds the text into a navigable object rather than a stream.
engagement_markers.caution: Cross-references are a maintenance liability — every one must survive reordering.

self_mention_and_stance.name: authorial I
self_mention_and_stance.definition: First-person singular self-reference by the writer.
self_mention_and_stance.example: I read the file twice before I believed the dates.
self_mention_and_stance.effect: Puts a person behind the judgment; in reported nonfiction it also discloses method.
self_mention_and_stance.caution: Register-defining and hard to reverse; decide before drafting whether the book has an I.

self_mention_and_stance.name: editorial we
self_mention_and_stance.definition: First-person plural standing for a single author or an institutional voice.
self_mention_and_stance.example: We turn now to the second objection.
self_mention_and_stance.effect: Formal and impersonal; conventional in scholarly writing and stiff outside it.
self_mention_and_stance.caution: Easily confused with inclusive we, which invites the reader in rather than standing in for the author.

self_mention_and_stance.name: exclusive we
self_mention_and_stance.definition: First-person plural referring to the writer's team or institution, not the reader.
self_mention_and_stance.example: We reviewed 14,000 filings for this chapter.
self_mention_and_stance.effect: Reports collective work and establishes the evidentiary base.

self_mention_and_stance.name: impersonal self-reference
self_mention_and_stance.definition: Referring to oneself in the third person or as the text.
self_mention_and_stance.effect: Maximum distance; the text rather than the person carries the claim.
self_mention_and_stance.caution: Chapters do not argue and studies do not find; sustained use makes prose agentless in a way readers feel as evasion.

self_mention_and_stance.name: announcement of purpose
self_mention_and_stance.definition: Explicitly stating what the writer will do next or in the work as a whole.
self_mention_and_stance.example: I will argue that the delay was the policy, not a failure of it.
self_mention_and_stance.effect: Contracts with the reader; makes the book auditable against its own promise.

self_mention_and_stance.name: positionality statement
self_mention_and_stance.definition: Disclosing the writer's stake, standpoint, or conflict of interest.
self_mention_and_stance.example: I worked for one of the firms in chapter six; that chapter names it.
self_mention_and_stance.effect: Converts a discoverable bias into a credential for candor.
self_mention_and_stance.caution: A disclosure is not a defense; it does not license the bias it names.

self_mention_and_stance.name: self-deprecation
self_mention_and_stance.definition: Undercutting one's own authority or performance in passing.
self_mention_and_stance.example: It took me four years to notice what a paralegal saw in an afternoon.
self_mention_and_stance.effect: Lowers the reader's defenses and makes subsequent confident claims easier to accept.
self_mention_and_stance.caution: In excess it becomes a bid for reassurance and undermines the argument for real.

self_mention_and_stance.name: self-citation
self_mention_and_stance.definition: Reference to the writer's own prior work.
self_mention_and_stance.example: I set out the earlier version of this argument in a 2019 paper.
self_mention_and_stance.effect: Establishes track record and points readers to the fuller treatment.
self_mention_and_stance.caution: A visible ratio; more than a handful in a trade book reads as self-promotion.

self_mention_and_stance.name: narrating I
self_mention_and_stance.definition: The first person used as a character moving through the reported world, not as the arguer.
self_mention_and_stance.example: The clerk slid the folder across the counter and asked if I was family.
self_mention_and_stance.effect: The immersive first person of literary journalism; carries scene rather than stance.
self_mention_and_stance.caution: Distinct from the authorial I, and mixing the two without signal confuses who is speaking.

precision_moves.name: exact figure
precision_moves.definition: Giving the specific number instead of a quantity word.
precision_moves.example: Not: a huge backlog. But: 41,388 unprocessed claims.
precision_moves.effect: A number is checkable, memorable, and does the emphatic work of an adjective without asking for trust.
precision_moves.caution: Only when you have it, and only at the precision your source supports.

precision_moves.name: order-of-magnitude anchor
precision_moves.definition: Translating a number into a unit the reader's body already knows.
precision_moves.example: enough paper to fill a shipping container; a delay longer than the war it was funding
precision_moves.effect: Converts an unfelt magnitude into a felt one; the standard move for numbers above human scale.
precision_moves.caution: The anchor must be accurate and familiar, or it teaches the wrong size.

precision_moves.name: proper noun
precision_moves.definition: Naming the specific person, place, company, or document rather than the category.
precision_moves.example: Not: a federal agency. But: the Bureau of Prisons.
precision_moves.effect: Every proper noun is an implicit claim that the writer did the work; generic nouns imply the opposite.

precision_moves.name: brand and model
precision_moves.definition: Naming the specific make of an object where the category would do.
precision_moves.example: not a station wagon but a rust-sided Country Squire
precision_moves.effect: Places the scene in a class, a decade, and a price bracket in three words.
precision_moves.caution: Brand detail dates a text deliberately; make sure that is what you want.

precision_moves.name: basic-level term
precision_moves.definition: Choosing the middle rung of the taxonomy — the level at which people naturally name things.
precision_moves.example: chair rather than furniture or Barcelona chair
precision_moves.effect: The fastest-processed and most imageable level; the right default unless expertise or precision demands otherwise.

precision_moves.name: subordinate-level term
precision_moves.definition: Dropping below the basic level to the specific kind.
precision_moves.example: elm rather than tree; sedge rather than grass
precision_moves.effect: Signals a narrator who knows the world they are describing, which buys credit for everything else.
precision_moves.caution: Unglossed specialist nouns exclude; one per paragraph is texture, five is a field guide.

precision_moves.name: term of art
precision_moves.definition: Deploying a discipline's defined term where the loose word would blur a real distinction.
precision_moves.example: consideration in contract law; standing in litigation; significance in statistics
precision_moves.effect: Buys precision and signals competence; each one should be introduced once and then used consistently.
precision_moves.caution: The trap is terms that look ordinary — readers will apply the everyday sense unless you say otherwise.

precision_moves.name: unit of measure
precision_moves.definition: Attaching an explicit unit to a quantity.
precision_moves.example: not high dosage but 400 milligrams a day for eleven months
precision_moves.effect: Makes a claim comparable and falsifiable; unitless quantities cannot be argued with or checked.

precision_moves.name: precise date
precision_moves.definition: Giving the day rather than the period.
precision_moves.example: Not: in the early nineties. But: on 6 March 1992.
precision_moves.effect: Dates create sequence, and sequence is where causal arguments live.
precision_moves.caution: Precision implies a source. A dated claim invites a footnote.

precision_moves.name: price
precision_moves.definition: Attaching the cost, in the currency and terms of the time, and adjusting where comparison matters.
precision_moves.effect: Money is the most universally legible measure of scale a reader has.

precision_moves.name: in-line source naming
precision_moves.definition: Naming the source inside the sentence rather than only in a note.
precision_moves.example: The inspector general's 2019 report put the figure at eleven.
precision_moves.effect: Lets the reader weigh the evidence as they read it instead of deferring to a note they will not turn to.

precision_moves.name: telling detail
precision_moves.definition: One specific particular chosen so it implies the whole scene or character.
precision_moves.example: the receipts still rubber-banded by month
precision_moves.effect: Synecdoche as reporting; a single observed detail outperforms a paragraph of summary description.
precision_moves.caution: It must be observed, not invented, in nonfiction — and it must actually be typical, or it lies.

precision_moves.name: le mot juste
precision_moves.definition: Discriminating among near-synonyms for the one that carries the exact sense, connotation, and register.
precision_moves.example: reluctant, unwilling, hesitant, loath — four different states
precision_moves.effect: The difference between a sentence that means something and a sentence that gestures at a meaning.
precision_moves.caution: Discriminating is not the same as reaching for the rarer word; the exact word is often the plain one.

precision_moves.name: calibrated qualifier
precision_moves.definition: Choosing a qualifier that matches the actual strength of the evidence.
precision_moves.example: consistent with, rather than proves; suggests, rather than shows
precision_moves.effect: Precision about confidence is a form of precision; readers who catch one overclaim discount everything after it.

precision_moves.name: operational definition
precision_moves.definition: Defining a term by the procedure used to measure or identify it.
precision_moves.example: By delay I mean any interval longer than the statutory thirty days, counted from the filing stamp.
precision_moves.effect: Turns an arguable word into a countable one and forecloses definitional disputes.

precision_moves.name: stipulative definition
precision_moves.definition: Declaring how a term will be used in this text, without claiming that is its general meaning.
precision_moves.example: I use failure here in the narrow sense of a missed contractual deadline.
precision_moves.effect: Buys a shorthand for the rest of the book at the cost of one sentence.
precision_moves.caution: Stipulating a sense that conflicts with common usage guarantees readers will drift back to their own.

precision_moves.name: definition by negation
precision_moves.definition: Fixing a term's boundary by saying what it excludes.
precision_moves.example: This is not a story about fraud. Nobody stole anything.
precision_moves.effect: Clears away the reading the reader was about to default to; especially useful for loaded subjects.

precision_moves.name: sensory particular
precision_moves.definition: Naming a specific perceptible property — color, sound, texture, smell — rather than a general one.
precision_moves.example: not old paper but paper gone the color of weak tea
precision_moves.effect: Concrete sensory nouns and adjectives are the raw material of imageability.
precision_moves.caution: One sense per sentence; stacked sensory detail reads as inventory.

precision_moves.name: false precision
precision_moves.definition: Reporting more decimal places, or a narrower figure, than the evidence supports.
precision_moves.example: a 37.4 percent increase derived from two rounded inputs
precision_moves.effect: Looks rigorous and is not; a numerate reader who catches it discounts the whole chapter.
precision_moves.caution: Round to the precision of your least precise input, and say where the number came from.

verb_strength_moves.name: strong verb over verb plus adverb
verb_strength_moves.definition: Replacing a weak verb modified by an adverb with a single verb that contains the manner.
verb_strength_moves.example: walked slowly and heavily becomes trudged; said loudly becomes shouted
verb_strength_moves.effect: One word instead of two, and the manner becomes part of the action instead of a comment on it.
verb_strength_moves.caution: Not a blanket rule — sometimes the adverb carries information the verb cannot, and hunting -ly words mechanically damages good sentences.

verb_strength_moves.name: light verb unpacking
verb_strength_moves.definition: Collapsing a light verb plus nominalization into the verb hiding inside it.
verb_strength_moves.example: make a decision becomes decide; conduct an investigation becomes investigate; provide assistance becomes help
verb_strength_moves.effect: Cuts two or three words and restores the action to the verb slot, where readers look for it.

verb_strength_moves.name: buried verb recovery
verb_strength_moves.definition: Finding the action that has been turned into an abstract noun and making it the sentence's verb again.
verb_strength_moves.example: The implementation of the reduction was undertaken becomes They cut it.
verb_strength_moves.effect: The single highest-yield revision move in institutional prose; usually restores the missing agent at the same time.

verb_strength_moves.name: denominal verb
verb_strength_moves.definition: Using a noun as a verb.
verb_strength_moves.example: to shoulder, to table, to weather, to landfill
verb_strength_moves.effect: Compresses a whole action into a familiar object and gives prose a physical, idiomatic edge.
verb_strength_moves.caution: Fresh denominals from corporate register (to action, to solution) read as jargon; the tolerance is a live style dispute.

verb_strength_moves.name: copula reduction
verb_strength_moves.definition: Lowering the proportion of sentences whose main verb is a form of to be.
verb_strength_moves.example: There was a delay in the shipment becomes The shipment sat in Newark for six weeks.
verb_strength_moves.effect: Forces a real predicate; a paragraph with no verbs but is and was reports states and never events.
verb_strength_moves.caution: To be is not a defect — identity and definition genuinely need it. The target is the ratio, not the word.

verb_strength_moves.name: expletive excision
verb_strength_moves.definition: Removing there is, there are, and it is when they occupy the subject and verb slots without content.
verb_strength_moves.example: There are three reasons the audit failed becomes The audit failed for three reasons.
verb_strength_moves.effect: Recovers the sentence's real subject and typically saves three words.
verb_strength_moves.caution: Existential there is sometimes exactly right — it introduces something into the scene.

verb_strength_moves.name: active over passive
verb_strength_moves.definition: Choosing the active voice so the agent occupies the subject position.
verb_strength_moves.example: The rule was waived becomes The regional director waived the rule.
verb_strength_moves.effect: Restores agency and usually shortens the clause.
verb_strength_moves.caution: Passive is right when the agent is unknown, irrelevant, or genuinely less important than the patient. The fault is the agentless passive used to hide someone.

verb_strength_moves.name: agentive subject
verb_strength_moves.definition: Making the sentence's grammatical subject the entity that actually acts.
verb_strength_moves.example: Not: The policy resulted in delays. But: Clerks stopped processing claims after four.
verb_strength_moves.effect: Aligns grammar with causation; abstractions cannot do things, and sentences that say they do obscure who did.

verb_strength_moves.name: specific motion verb
verb_strength_moves.definition: Selecting the verb that specifies manner of movement.
verb_strength_moves.example: walk / trudge / lope / stride / shuffle / pick his way
verb_strength_moves.effect: Carries characterization, terrain, and emotional state in the predicate rather than in description around it.

verb_strength_moves.name: precise perception verb
verb_strength_moves.definition: Choosing among the fine-grained verbs of looking, hearing, and touching.
verb_strength_moves.example: glance, stare, glimpse, scan, study, watch
verb_strength_moves.effect: Duration and intention are built into the verb; watched for an hour and glimpsed are different events, not different intensities.

verb_strength_moves.name: filter verb removal
verb_strength_moves.definition: Cutting the perception verb that stands between the reader and the perceived thing.
verb_strength_moves.example: She saw the door standing open becomes The door stood open.
verb_strength_moves.effect: Removes a layer of mediation and moves the reader from watching a character perceive to perceiving directly.
verb_strength_moves.caution: Keep the filter when whose perception it is matters, or when unreliability is the point.

verb_strength_moves.name: transitive strengthening
verb_strength_moves.definition: Giving a verb a direct object so the action lands on something.
verb_strength_moves.example: The company reorganized becomes The company cut the claims unit to nine people.
verb_strength_moves.effect: Makes consequence visible; intransitive verbs let events happen to no one.

verb_strength_moves.name: speech verb selection
verb_strength_moves.definition: Choosing among said and its alternatives on purpose.
verb_strength_moves.example: said, asked, told, admitted, conceded, insisted
verb_strength_moves.effect: Said is invisible and neutral; anything else is a claim about the speaker's state or the truth of what they say.
verb_strength_moves.caution: Substituting synonyms for said to avoid repetition is elegant variation in its purest form; readers notice quipped and stop reading the dialogue.

verb_strength_moves.name: aspect choice
verb_strength_moves.definition: Using progressive, perfect, or simple aspect to shape how an event sits in time.
verb_strength_moves.example: He signed / He was signing / He had signed
verb_strength_moves.effect: Simple aspect gives discrete events, progressive gives duration and interruptibility, perfect gives consequence in the present.

verb_strength_moves.name: historical present
verb_strength_moves.definition: Narrating past events in the present tense.
verb_strength_moves.example: He walks into the office and the file is already gone.
verb_strength_moves.effect: Immediacy and suspense; the outcome feels undecided.
verb_strength_moves.caution: Exhausting over a long stretch, and awkward to escape — switching back mid-chapter is jarring.

verb_strength_moves.name: imperative attack
verb_strength_moves.definition: Opening a sentence with a verb in the imperative, putting the stress on the first syllable.
verb_strength_moves.effect: Fastest possible sentence start; no subject to wade through before the action.

verb_strength_moves.name: modal stripping
verb_strength_moves.definition: Removing hedging auxiliaries that add no meaning to the verb.
verb_strength_moves.example: would tend to suggest becomes suggests; can be seen to be becomes is
verb_strength_moves.effect: Recovers directness; the surviving modals then carry real epistemic weight.

verb_strength_moves.name: metaphor-carrying verb
verb_strength_moves.definition: Locating the figure in the verb rather than in an adjective or a simile.
verb_strength_moves.effect: The most economical form of metaphor; no comparison has to be announced.
verb_strength_moves.caution: Two verb-metaphors from different domains in one sentence is a mixed metaphor even when no noun is involved.

verb_strength_moves.name: verb-first inversion
verb_strength_moves.definition: Fronting the verb or its particle ahead of the subject for rhythm and emphasis.
verb_strength_moves.example: Gone were the paper files. Out came the second ledger.
verb_strength_moves.effect: Marked and slightly archaic; strong once, mannered twice.

naming_strategies.name: specific naming
naming_strategies.definition: Referring to a thing by its own name rather than by a category label.
naming_strategies.example: the Ely Street depot, not the facility
naming_strategies.effect: The reader can hold a named thing in memory across a chapter; a category label evaporates.

naming_strategies.name: coinage
naming_strategies.definition: Inventing a term for a concept the language does not have a word for.
naming_strategies.example: Naming a recurring pattern so the rest of the book can refer to it in two words.
naming_strategies.effect: A well-made coinage is the most durable thing a nonfiction book can leave behind.
naming_strategies.caution: It must name something real that recurs, be pronounceable, and be defined once and used consistently. Coinages for things that already have names are vanity.

naming_strategies.name: capitalized concept
naming_strategies.definition: Capitalizing an ordinary noun to mark it as the book's technical term.
naming_strategies.effect: Flags a defined sense without inventing a word.
naming_strategies.caution: Reads as portentous quickly; more than two capitalized concepts in a book and the reader stops tracking them.

naming_strategies.name: acronym management
naming_strategies.definition: Spelling out an initialism at first use and then using it consistently — or refusing it and using a plain short form.
naming_strategies.example: the Office of Special Counsel (OSC) — or, better, the counsel's office throughout
naming_strategies.effect: Acronyms cost the reader a lookup every time; a plain short form costs nothing.
naming_strategies.caution: Three or more live acronyms in a chapter exceeds most readers' working memory.

naming_strategies.name: eponym
naming_strategies.definition: Naming a thing after a person associated with it.
naming_strategies.example: Goodhart's law; the Dunning-Kruger effect; a boycott
naming_strategies.effect: Attaches a story to a concept, which makes the concept memorable.
naming_strategies.caution: Eponyms encode credit, and the credit is often historically wrong.

naming_strategies.name: name sound symbolism
naming_strategies.definition: Choosing a name whose phonetics fit the referent's character.
naming_strategies.caution: Broad in comic registers; in realist fiction the effect must be subtle enough to deny.

naming_strategies.name: place-name texture
naming_strategies.definition: Using real or plausible toponyms with the right regional phonology.
naming_strategies.example: county names with the right suffixes; streets that sound like the town's founding era
naming_strategies.effect: Grounds a setting more reliably than description does, because names carry history.

naming_strategies.name: epithet
naming_strategies.definition: A fixed descriptive tag attached to a name and repeated.
naming_strategies.example: swift-footed Achilles; the auditor with the yellow legal pad
naming_strategies.effect: Gives a minor figure a handle the reader can retrieve dozens of pages later.
naming_strategies.caution: Repeating the tag every mention is Homeric; in prose fiction twice is usually enough.

naming_strategies.name: sobriquet
naming_strategies.definition: A nickname used in place of the formal name.
naming_strategies.example: what the staff called the room, versus what the sign on the door said
naming_strategies.effect: The gap between official and unofficial names is often the whole story of an institution.

naming_strategies.name: first-mention full form
naming_strategies.definition: Giving the complete name on first appearance and a consistent short form thereafter.
naming_strategies.example: Deputy Commissioner Elaine Ross, then Ross throughout
naming_strategies.effect: The convention readers expect; violating it in either direction costs comprehension.

naming_strategies.name: deliberate non-name
naming_strategies.definition: Withholding a name and using a definite description instead.
naming_strategies.example: the man from the ministry; the company that bought the debt
naming_strategies.effect: Generalizes, or withholds identity for suspense, or protects a source.
naming_strategies.caution: In nonfiction an unnamed actor should be unnamed for a stated reason; readers assume the reason is that you do not know.

naming_strategies.name: term consistency
naming_strategies.definition: Using exactly one term for one concept throughout a text.
naming_strategies.example: Deciding once between claimant, applicant, and beneficiary, and never varying.
naming_strategies.effect: Readers treat a changed word as a changed thing; consistency is what makes technical prose followable.
naming_strategies.caution: Directly opposed to elegant variation, and the opposition is real: variety is a virtue in narration and a defect in terminology.

naming_strategies.name: style sheet entry
naming_strategies.definition: Recording each naming decision — spelling, capitalization, short form, gloss — in a running list as the draft proceeds.
naming_strategies.example: a two-column sheet of terms and the chosen form
naming_strategies.effect: The only reliable way to keep naming consistent across a book-length manuscript and a copy edit.

naming_strategies.name: metonymic naming
naming_strategies.definition: Referring to an institution or group by an associated place or object.
naming_strategies.example: Washington, the Street, the bench, City Hall
naming_strategies.caution: Also a way to avoid saying who; the metonym has no address and cannot be held responsible.

naming_strategies.name: label versus description
naming_strategies.definition: The choice between attaching a category label to someone and describing what they did.
naming_strategies.example: a fraudster, versus a man who signed his mother's name to nine checks
naming_strategies.effect: The label is shorter and does the reader's judging for them; the description is longer and more persuasive.
naming_strategies.caution: Labels are also legally riskier — description survives a defamation review that a label may not.

naming_strategies.name: pseudonymization
naming_strategies.definition: Replacing a real name with a stated pseudonym or an initial to protect a source.
naming_strategies.example: I have changed the names of the two clerks; nothing else about them is altered.
naming_strategies.effect: Preserves the reporting while limiting harm.
naming_strategies.caution: Disclose the practice explicitly at first use or in a note — undisclosed pseudonyms are a nonfiction integrity failure.

diction_faults.name: elegant variation
diction_faults.definition: Substituting synonyms for a repeated word purely to avoid repeating it (Fowler's term).
diction_faults.example: the report... the document... the paper... the aforementioned study
diction_faults.effect: Readers assume a new word means a new thing and start looking for the difference.
diction_faults.caution: Repeat the plain word. The rule reverses for narration, where a third the man in a paragraph is its own fault; the test is whether the word is a term.

diction_faults.name: thesaurus-itis
