diction_faults.definition: Reaching for the less common synonym on the assumption that rarer means better.
diction_faults.example: utilize, commence, endeavor, cognizant where use, start, try, aware were meant
diction_faults.effect: Inflates register, blurs sense, and signals a writer performing rather than communicating.
diction_faults.caution: Near-synonyms differ in connotation, collocation, and register; a thesaurus lists none of those.

diction_faults.name: near-miss word
diction_faults.definition: A word whose general sense fits but whose specific sense does not.
diction_faults.example: refute for dispute; disinterested for uninterested; fulsome for full; enormity for enormousness
diction_faults.effect: Readers who know the distinction lose confidence in every other word choice on the page.

diction_faults.name: false friend
diction_faults.definition: A word borrowed from another language whose English sense diverges from the source.
diction_faults.example: actual (not current); eventual (not possible); sensible (not sensitive)
diction_faults.effect: A reliable marker of translated or non-native text; also a hazard when quoting from translation.

diction_faults.name: malapropism
diction_faults.definition: Substituting a similar-sounding word for the intended one.
diction_faults.example: a pineapple of politeness, for pinnacle
diction_faults.effect: Comic when deliberate and characterizing in dialogue; simply an error otherwise.

diction_faults.name: jargon creep
diction_faults.definition: Progressive infiltration of a field's shorthand into passages written for a general audience.
diction_faults.example: A chapter that opens in plain English and ends in undefined acronyms and terms of art.
diction_faults.effect: Readers drop away one term at a time without noticing when they stopped following.
diction_faults.caution: Reread a drafted chapter counting undefined specialist terms; the count almost always climbs toward the end.

diction_faults.name: noun string
diction_faults.definition: Three or more nouns stacked as modifiers of a final noun.
diction_faults.example: quality improvement outcome measurement framework
diction_faults.effect: The reader must guess which nouns modify which; grammar gives no help.
diction_faults.caution: Unstack with prepositions and verbs: a framework for measuring whether quality improved.

diction_faults.name: abstraction lock
diction_faults.definition: Sustaining a passage entirely at the top of the ladder of abstraction, never touching a concrete instance.
diction_faults.example: Three paragraphs on institutional accountability mechanisms with no institution, no mechanism, and no person.
diction_faults.effect: The reader nods along and retains nothing; the argument becomes unfalsifiable because it never touches a case.
diction_faults.caution: Rule of thumb: no more than two consecutive sentences without a concrete noun.

diction_faults.name: of-chain
diction_faults.definition: A noun phrase built from a chain of of-prepositions.
diction_faults.example: the review of the implementation of the recommendations of the panel
diction_faults.effect: Each of forces the reader to hold another relation open; three is the practical limit and two is plenty.
diction_faults.caution: Fix by making one of the nouns a verb.

diction_faults.name: wordy connective
diction_faults.definition: A multi-word phrase doing the work of a single conjunction or preposition.
cues: in spite of the fact that
diction_faults.example: due to the fact that becomes because
diction_faults.effect: Pure padding at the joints of the argument, where the reader most needs speed.

diction_faults.name: elongated variant
diction_faults.definition: The longer form of a word or phrase used where the short form is exact.
diction_faults.example: prior to becomes before
diction_faults.effect: Adds syllables and a faint whiff of officialdom without adding meaning.
diction_faults.caution: Methodology and utilize do have proper technical senses; the fault is using them as elevated synonyms.

diction_faults.name: circumlocution
diction_faults.definition: Taking a phrase to say what a word says.
diction_faults.example: individuals of advanced age; at an early juncture; in a situation where funds are limited
diction_faults.effect: Distances and dilutes; frequently a symptom of avoiding the blunt word on purpose.

diction_faults.name: pleonasm
diction_faults.definition: Using more words than the sense requires, typically a modifier already contained in its head.
diction_faults.example: free gift, advance planning, past history, end result, revert back, close proximity
diction_faults.effect: Each is invisible individually and cumulatively makes prose feel padded.

diction_faults.name: tautology
diction_faults.definition: Restating the same proposition in different words as though it added something.
diction_faults.example: The reason it failed is because it did not work.
diction_faults.effect: Occupies the space where an explanation should be.
diction_faults.caution: Common at the end of hard paragraphs, where a writer restates rather than concludes.

diction_faults.name: redundant category word
diction_faults.definition: Naming the category of a word that already implies it.
diction_faults.example: red in color, large in size, at the present time, in the field of medicine, a period of two weeks
diction_faults.effect: One of the highest-frequency sources of wordiness and one of the easiest to cut mechanically.

diction_faults.name: vague quantifier
diction_faults.definition: A quantity word that conveys no quantity.
diction_faults.example: a number of complaints
diction_faults.effect: Signals either that the writer does not know the number or that the number is unimpressive.
diction_faults.caution: If you have the figure, give it. If you do not, say so.

diction_faults.name: unanchored this
diction_faults.definition: A demonstrative pronoun opening a sentence with no clear antecedent.
diction_faults.example: This meant the schedule slipped. (This what?)
diction_faults.effect: The reader has to reconstruct the referent from the previous sentence, and different readers reconstruct differently.
diction_faults.caution: Fix by supplying the noun: This delay meant...

diction_faults.name: filler adverb
diction_faults.definition: Adverbs that occupy a slot without modifying anything.
diction_faults.example: It was actually quite basically a failure.
diction_faults.effect: Reads as spoken hesitation transcribed; each one dilutes the word it precedes.

diction_faults.name: adverb dependence
diction_faults.definition: Relying on adverbs to supply intensity or manner that the verb and the evidence should carry.
diction_faults.example: moved quickly, said angrily, dramatically increased
diction_faults.effect: The adverb tells the reader what to conclude instead of giving them the grounds.
diction_faults.caution: Not a ban — the fault is the pattern, not the part of speech. Count the -ly words per page before deciding.

diction_faults.name: adjective stacking
diction_faults.definition: Piling multiple adjectives before a noun.
diction_faults.example: a bleak, gray, unforgiving, institutional corridor
diction_faults.effect: Each adjective dilutes the others; four modifiers produce a vaguer image than one exact one.
diction_faults.caution: Cut to the one that carries information the noun does not.

diction_faults.name: cliche
diction_faults.definition: A phrase whose figurative force has been used up by repetition.
diction_faults.example: at the end of the day, a perfect storm, the tip of the iceberg, level playing field
diction_faults.effect: Reads as filler and signals that the writer did not look at the thing being described.
diction_faults.caution: Cliches are hardest to see in one's own drafting because they arrive fluently; they are exactly what a fluency-optimized generator produces most.

diction_faults.name: doublespeak
diction_faults.definition: Language constructed to make an unwelcome reality unrecognizable.
diction_faults.example: revenue enhancement for tax increase; involuntary separation for layoff
diction_faults.effect: The reader either misses the meaning or notices the evasion and distrusts the source.
diction_faults.caution: Quote it, name it, and translate it. Never adopt it into your own narration.

diction_faults.name: purple diction
diction_faults.definition: Ornate, emotionally overpitched vocabulary applied to ordinary material.
diction_faults.example: The luminous cascade of morning gilded the humble breakfast table.
diction_faults.effect: The prose asks for a response the subject has not earned; readers feel manipulated.

diction_faults.name: euphemism creep
diction_faults.definition: Adopting an institution's softening vocabulary as the text's own default.
diction_faults.example: A book about layoffs that says restructuring throughout.
diction_faults.effect: Silently transfers the institution's framing into supposedly neutral narration.
diction_faults.caution: Decide once per book which term you will use and state why in a note if it is contested.

diction_faults.name: weasel word
diction_faults.definition: A qualifier that appears to add precision while draining the claim of content.
diction_faults.example: Studies show the program helps to reduce costs by up to 40 percent.
diction_faults.effect: Every element is technically defensible and the sentence asserts nothing.
diction_faults.caution: Named for the weasel's reputed trick of sucking out an egg and leaving the shell intact.

diction_faults.name: hollow abstraction
diction_faults.definition: Abstract nouns of approval strung together in place of a claim.
diction_faults.example: innovative solutions delivering meaningful impact at scale
diction_faults.effect: Cannot be disagreed with because nothing has been said.
diction_faults.caution: Test: negate the sentence. If nobody would assert the negation, the original said nothing.

diction_faults.name: slop lexicon
diction_faults.definition: A cluster of words and phrases that machine-generated prose overproduces relative to edited human writing.
diction_faults.example: This rich tapestry of interconnected challenges underscores the crucial need to navigate a complex landscape.
diction_faults.effect: Instantly recognizable to editors and to detectors; the vocabulary of fluency without observation.
diction_faults.caution: The list moves. Maintain it as a repo-level ban list from measurement rather than from memory, and check candidates against the actual corpus before banning.

diction_faults.name: anthropomorphized abstraction
diction_faults.definition: Giving intentions and actions to entities that cannot have them.
diction_faults.example: The data wants to be free. The market decided. The algorithm believes.
diction_faults.effect: Hides the humans who chose, which is sometimes the point and always a claim.
diction_faults.caution: Distinct from deliberate personification: the fault is the metaphor the writer did not notice making.

diction_faults.name: Latinate connective chain
diction_faults.definition: Successive paragraphs opened with heavy formal connectives.
diction_faults.example: Moreover... Furthermore... Additionally...
diction_faults.effect: Signals that the writer is listing rather than arguing; the connectives assert a relation the content does not supply.
diction_faults.caution: A measurable tell in both student and machine prose. Replace with a transition that names the actual relation, or with nothing.

figurative_diction_controls.name: tenor and vehicle
figurative_diction_controls.definition: Richards's terms for the two halves of a metaphor: the subject (tenor) and the thing it is described in terms of (vehicle).
figurative_diction_controls.example: In the mind is a machine, mind is the tenor and machine the vehicle.
figurative_diction_controls.effect: Gives a vocabulary for diagnosing a bad figure — usually the vehicle is wrong, not the idea.

figurative_diction_controls.name: controlling metaphor
figurative_diction_controls.definition: One governing figure sustained through a passage, chapter, or book, with subsequent language drawn from its domain.
figurative_diction_controls.example: A book about a bureaucracy figured throughout as a plumbing system: pressure, backflow, capacity.
figurative_diction_controls.effect: Gives a long text conceptual coherence readers feel without naming.
figurative_diction_controls.caution: It must be chosen deliberately, or an accidental one will emerge and constrain you anyway.

figurative_diction_controls.name: vehicle domain consistency
figurative_diction_controls.definition: Keeping successive figures in one source domain within a passage.
figurative_diction_controls.example: If the argument is nautical, do not switch to farming three sentences later.
figurative_diction_controls.effect: Consistency lets images accumulate; inconsistency makes each one cancel the last.

figurative_diction_controls.name: domain-native imagery
figurative_diction_controls.definition: Drawing the vehicle from the world the subject actually inhabits.
figurative_diction_controls.example: Describing a fisherman's fatigue in terms of tide and net rather than of office deadlines.
figurative_diction_controls.effect: The figure earns its place twice — as image and as characterization of whose perception it is.

figurative_diction_controls.name: metaphor reanimation
figurative_diction_controls.definition: Reviving a dead metaphor by extending or literalizing it.
figurative_diction_controls.example: The department had branches, and like branches they grew where the light was.
figurative_diction_controls.effect: Recovers force from a phrase the reader was about to skim.
figurative_diction_controls.caution: Only worth doing when the revived image does argumentative work; otherwise it is a joke about vocabulary.

figurative_diction_controls.name: metaphor density budget
figurative_diction_controls.definition: A deliberate limit on how many live figures a passage carries.
figurative_diction_controls.example: One developed figure per page in expository nonfiction; more in lyric passages.
figurative_diction_controls.effect: Scarcity is what makes a figure land; in a metaphor-saturated page no single image is visible.

figurative_diction_controls.name: simile and metaphor choice
figurative_diction_controls.definition: The decision to mark a comparison with like or as, or to assert identity.
figurative_diction_controls.example: The room was like a cell / The room was a cell.
figurative_diction_controls.effect: Simile keeps the two things separate and invites inspection of the likeness; metaphor fuses them and asserts.
figurative_diction_controls.caution: Simile is safer and weaker; a page of similes reads as a writer unwilling to commit.

figurative_diction_controls.name: literalization risk
figurative_diction_controls.definition: The danger that a figure will be read straight, especially in factual or technical contexts.
figurative_diction_controls.example: Calling a merger a bloodbath in a chapter that also describes an actual injury.
figurative_diction_controls.effect: Comic or confusing collision between figurative and literal registers.
figurative_diction_controls.caution: Highest risk in nonfiction about violence, illness, and money, where every vehicle has a literal counterpart in the material.

figurative_diction_controls.name: deliberate catachresis
figurative_diction_controls.definition: A knowingly wrong or strained application of a word, used for effect.
figurative_diction_controls.effect: Forces the reader to construct a meaning the language does not supply.
figurative_diction_controls.caution: Distinguishable from an error only if the surrounding prose is visibly in control.

figurative_diction_controls.name: hyperbole calibration
figurative_diction_controls.definition: Choosing the degree of overstatement and keeping it consistent so readers know how to discount.
figurative_diction_controls.example: An overstatement inside a scrupulously literal chapter reads as an error, not a figure.
figurative_diction_controls.effect: Readers calibrate to a text's exaggeration level within a page and read everything after against it.

figurative_diction_controls.name: personification restraint
figurative_diction_controls.definition: Limiting the attribution of human agency to non-human subjects to places where it does real work.
figurative_diction_controls.example: The house waited, as houses do — used once, in a chapter about return.
figurative_diction_controls.effect: Powerful in isolation, cloying in quantity.
figurative_diction_controls.caution: Distinct from anthropomorphized abstraction: the fault is unnoticed agency, the device is chosen agency.

figurative_diction_controls.name: synesthesia
figurative_diction_controls.definition: Describing one sense in the vocabulary of another.
figurative_diction_controls.example: a loud shirt; a sharp cheese; a warm voice
figurative_diction_controls.effect: Compresses a complex impression into a short phrase; many instances are already idiomatic and therefore invisible.

figurative_diction_controls.name: concrete vehicle rule
figurative_diction_controls.definition: The working rule that the vehicle should be more concrete than the tenor.
figurative_diction_controls.example: An argument as a building, not a building as an argument.
figurative_diction_controls.effect: Metaphor works by explaining the less known in terms of the better known; reversing the direction produces fog.

figurative_diction_controls.name: decorative figure
figurative_diction_controls.definition: A figure added for texture rather than for meaning.
figurative_diction_controls.example: A simile in the opening line that never connects to anything after it.
figurative_diction_controls.effect: Costs the reader attention and returns nothing.
figurative_diction_controls.caution: Test each figure by deleting it. If the paragraph loses only prettiness, leave it deleted.

period_and_dialect_diction.name: archaism
period_and_dialect_diction.definition: A word or form no longer in current use, deployed deliberately.
period_and_dialect_diction.effect: Evokes a period or an elevated register in a single word.
period_and_dialect_diction.caution: One archaism reads as texture; three read as costume.

period_and_dialect_diction.name: anachronistic diction
period_and_dialect_diction.definition: Vocabulary that did not exist, or did not carry the modern sense, in the period depicted.
period_and_dialect_diction.example: A character in 1890 describing a system as stressed, or a scene set in 1935 using teenager.
period_and_dialect_diction.effect: Breaks the historical frame for any reader who knows.
period_and_dialect_diction.caution: Check the first-attestation date and the sense date, not just the word — many old words acquired their modern meanings recently.

period_and_dialect_diction.name: period lexicon check
period_and_dialect_diction.definition: Systematically dating the vocabulary of a historical passage against a dictionary with attestation dates.
period_and_dialect_diction.example: Running the nouns and verbs of a scene through the OED's first-use dates.
period_and_dialect_diction.effect: The only reliable way to catch anachronism, which is invisible to the ear.
period_and_dialect_diction.caution: Absolute period fidelity is unreadable; the goal is nothing that jars, not nothing post-dating the scene.

period_and_dialect_diction.name: faux-antique diction
period_and_dialect_diction.definition: Invented old-sounding language assembled from a handful of markers.
period_and_dialect_diction.example: forsooth, methinks, prithee sprinkled over otherwise modern syntax
period_and_dialect_diction.effect: Reads as pastiche, because period voice lives in syntax and idiom, not in a few flagged words.
period_and_dialect_diction.caution: The convincing route is modern-legible syntax with period-accurate concrete nouns.

period_and_dialect_diction.name: eye dialect
period_and_dialect_diction.definition: Nonstandard spelling of standard pronunciations to mark a speaker as uneducated.
period_and_dialect_diction.effect: Marks class rather than sound, since everyone says wuz.
period_and_dialect_diction.caution: Widely regarded as condescending and slows every reader; use lexicon, idiom, and syntax instead.

period_and_dialect_diction.name: regionalism
period_and_dialect_diction.definition: Vocabulary specific to a geographic speech community.
period_and_dialect_diction.example: pop / soda / coke; bubbler; pavement versus sidewalk; wee
period_and_dialect_diction.effect: Places a speaker geographically in one word, without any respelling.

period_and_dialect_diction.name: sociolect
period_and_dialect_diction.definition: Vocabulary marking social class, occupation, or institutional position.
period_and_dialect_diction.example: The difference between how the ward clerk, the attending, and the family describe the same event.
period_and_dialect_diction.effect: The most efficient way to show a hierarchy: let each level name the same thing differently.

period_and_dialect_diction.name: idiolect
period_and_dialect_diction.definition: The individual speech signature of one character — favored words, tics, syntactic habits.
period_and_dialect_diction.example: A character who says fine to mean everything from agreement to fury.
period_and_dialect_diction.effect: Lets dialogue be attributed without tags and makes a voice recognizable across a book.
period_and_dialect_diction.caution: A tic repeated every appearance stops being characterization and becomes a label.

period_and_dialect_diction.name: generational marker
period_and_dialect_diction.definition: Vocabulary that dates a speaker to a cohort rather than a place or class.
period_and_dialect_diction.example: icebox, dial the phone, tape it, roll down the window
period_and_dialect_diction.effect: Ages a character precisely, often without stating an age.
period_and_dialect_diction.caution: Also dates the writer when used unawares in narration.

period_and_dialect_diction.name: dated technical vocabulary
period_and_dialect_diction.definition: Terms from a field's earlier state of the art.
period_and_dialect_diction.example: wireless, electronic brain, data processing, motorcar
period_and_dialect_diction.effect: Period-accurate and often quietly funny; also a way to mark how much a field has moved.
period_and_dialect_diction.caution: Gloss on first use if the modern reader cannot recover the referent.

period_and_dialect_diction.name: translationese
period_and_dialect_diction.definition: Diction that follows the source language's idiom or word class rather than natural English.
period_and_dialect_diction.example: Overuse of abstract nouns and of the definite article in translated academic prose.
period_and_dialect_diction.effect: Fluent-looking English that is subtly not idiomatic; readers feel it as fog without locating it.
period_and_dialect_diction.caution: The same signature appears in machine-generated prose and in text translated by machine.
